voiceover: Some Old Testament verses are about the LORD, and the LORD alone. Watch what the New Testament does with them. Psalm 102 is addressed to the LORD, the unchanging Creator. Hebrews chapter 1 applies it to the Son: You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning … you are the same, and your years will have no end. In Isaiah 45, the LORD swears: to me every knee shall bow. A hymn in Philippians 2, widely regarded as older than Paul's letter, says that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow — to the glory of God the Father. Joel promises: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. Paul quotes it in Romans 10, having just written that Jesus is Lord — and that the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him. And when Jesus forgives a man's sins, his critics object: who can forgive sins but God alone? He does not deny it. He answers by demonstration — he heals the man. The first Christians to apply these texts to Jesus, and to worship him, were Jewish believers who would have regarded worshipping any creature as blasphemy. So the New Testament does not add a second god beside the LORD. It includes Jesus within the unique identity of the one God of Israel. And the Word who was God became flesh.
